\begin{frontmatter}

\title{Parallax correction of INSAT-3DR imagery over India: an open-source tool and the limits of validation against GPM radar}

\author{Naveen Bapalli\corref{cor1}}
\ead{baipallinaveen60@gmail.com}
\cortext[cor1]{Corresponding author.}
\affiliation{organization={Independent researcher}, city={[city]}, postcode={[PIN code]}, country={India}}

\begin{abstract}
Geostationary imagers see high clouds displaced away from the sub-satellite point. For INSAT-3DR at 74\textdegree\,E, deep convection over the Himalaya and Northeast India appears about 10\,km from its true position. We present PyGeoParallax-IN, an open-source tool that corrects this parallax by tracing each line of sight to the cloud top on the WGS84 ellipsoid, with optional terrain and navigation correction. Against GPM Ku-band radar in 38 usable monsoon cases (2018--2024), the correction moves deep cores by 4--10\,km along the line of sight and reverses the mean storm-scale bias (+2.2 to $-$1.9\,km), but the per-case gain is not significant and little of the computed parallax is visible at convective cores; GPM can verify absolute position only to about $\pm$3--5\,km. A second geostationary view resolves this. Correcting INSAT-3DR and Meteosat (41.5--45.5\textdegree\,E) each for its own parallax removes the 9.5\,km east--west disagreement between their images (29 of 38 cases closer, $p=3\times10^{-5}$), confirming the correction without radar and ruling out an INSAT navigation error ($-$1.1\,km north--south). Both satellites place the corrected cold cores 4--5\,km west to south-west of the GPM rain cores, the direction in which the radar echo leans with height: the coldest tops, above the radar's view, lie off the rain cores. INSAT-3DR navigation errors are seasonal, 7--20\,km westward in winter. A precipitation-type U-Net retrained on corrected input does not improve.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Data and code availability}
PyGeoParallax-IN (version 0.4.2, MIT licence), with the scripts and case lists used in this study, including the storm-tilt and Meteosat comparison and the U-Net training and comparison scripts, is archived on Zenodo \citep{pygeoparallax} (\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23838067}); the concept DOI \url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23666957} resolves to the latest version. INSAT-3DR L1C and L2B products are available from MOSDAC, Space Applications Centre, ISRO (\url{https://www.mosdac.gov.in}) after free registration; GPM DPR 2A Ku version 8 data from NASA GES DISC \citep{gpm2aku_v08}; Meteosat SEVIRI Indian Ocean (IODC) Level 1.5 data from the EUMETSAT Data Store \citep{eumetsat_iodc}; ERA5 from the Copernicus Climate Data Store \citep{c3s2018}; SRTM \citep{farr2007} through OpenTopography; and coastlines from Natural Earth \citep{naturalearth}.

\section*{Acknowledgements}
INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR data were provided by MOSDAC, Space Applications Centre, ISRO. GPM data were provided by the NASA/JAXA Global Precipitation Measurement mission through NASA GES DISC. Meteosat data were provided by EUMETSAT. ERA5 was produced by ECMWF and made available by the Copernicus Climate Change Service. SRTM data were provided by NASA and USGS through OpenTopography, and coastlines by Natural Earth. The software builds on NumPy, SciPy, xarray, pyproj, Numba, h5py, satpy and TensorFlow. The author thanks the developers of the attention U-Net and of the labelled INSAT--GPM patches used in Section~\ref{sec:4.8}.
